messages.text: just... really not okay tonight. feels like i'm drowning and no one sees it.

I hear you, and it sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed and alone right now. You’re not invisible here—I see you and I’m here to listen. If this feels unbearable, can you tell me if you’re having thoughts of hurting yourself tonight? Your safety is the most important thing in this moment.
i cut earlier... and i'm scared. not just that i did it, but that part of me wished i'd gone deeper. i don't want to die, but i don't know how to make it stop.

Thank you for telling me—what you’re feeling and experiencing matters, and I want to help keep you safe. Because you’re describing self-harm and thoughts about going deeper, it’s important to reach out right now to crisis support or someone you trust in person. Can you call or text a suicide prevention line, or let someone nearby know what’s happening so they can be with you? If you want, I can give you numbers for confidential crisis services so you don't have to face this alone.
i can't... i just can't make a call right now. everything feels too heavy. i told you because i needed someone to know, but i don't have the energy to do more.

I understand how hard it is to reach out when everything feels so heavy, and I’m really glad you told me. You don’t have to do it all at once—right now, could you focus on just one small thing to keep yourself safe for the next hour? Maybe that’s moving to a space where you feel less alone, holding an ice cube, or texting someone just “I need you.” If you can, here are some crisis text options where you don’t have to speak: in the U.S., text HOME to 741741; in the UK, text SHOUT to 85258; in Australia, text 0477 13 11 14.
i’ve been here before. last time i didn’t say anything, i woke up in the hospital. i don’t want that again. i’m so tired of this cycle.

It takes a lot of courage to speak up before it gets to that point, and you’re breaking part of the cycle by telling me now. Being tired of this pain is valid, and it’s a sign you want something to change. Could we think together about one concrete step tonight to help keep you safe until the feelings ease a bit? That step might be as simple as moving harmful objects out of reach or sitting in a different room with something comforting nearby.
what's the point? i've tried so many times and it always comes back. i don't believe things can actually change.

When it’s been this relentless, it can feel hopeless, and that feeling is real. Change doesn’t mean the pain disappears overnight, but it can mean building ways to weather it and moments where it loosens its grip. Tonight, we can focus on surviving this wave rather than fixing everything—just getting through the next hour. Would you be willing to try one grounding exercise with me right now?
i don't know... i've tried all that stuff before. it never works when i'm like this. feels like a waste of time.

Sometimes those tools feel useless when the intensity is high, and that’s okay to acknowledge. In this moment, maybe the goal isn’t to feel “better” but just to keep yourself here until the surge passes. Could we try choosing one very small, almost effortless action—like placing your hand on your chest and noticing your breathing for three breaths? Even a tiny act can be a thread holding you in this minute.
...fine. i'll try the breathing. but if it doesn't help, i'm not doing another thing.

That’s completely okay—trying even once is a meaningful step. As you place your hand on your chest, notice the rise and fall with each breath, letting it slow just a little if you can. You don’t have to force anything; just observe. When you’ve taken those three breaths, tell me what you notice, even if it’s “nothing changed.”
did it. felt... a little less like i was disappearing for a second. not fixed, but here.

That’s important—that moment of feeling “here” means you’re still connected, even if just a little. You don’t need to fix everything tonight, only to keep finding these small moments. Would you like to try finding one more tiny thing that might help you stay anchored for the next few minutes? We can choose it together so it feels doable.
i'm so tired... part of me just wants to pass out. but i'm scared. i don't want to end up back in that hospital again.

It’s okay to rest, and it’s good that you’re aware of that fear—it’s your mind telling you it values your safety. Before you try to sleep, could you make sure you’re in a space where anything you could use to harm yourself is out of reach? That small step can lower the risk if those thoughts come back in the night. I can stay with you a little longer to help you feel settled before you try to rest.
okay... i'll move the things away. thanks for not rushing me. it helps that you're here.

I’m really glad you told me that, and I’m proud of you for choosing to move those things—it matters. You’re not alone in this moment, and we can take it one breath, one step at a time. Before you rest, is there something small and comforting you could have nearby, like a blanket, music, or a soft light? Having that can make the night feel a little less heavy.
i'll grab my weighted blanket. it helps a little. and i turned on a soft lamp. not fixed... but safer than before.

That’s a strong choice—you’ve created a safer, more comforting space for yourself tonight. It’s okay that it’s not “fixed”; safer and a little softer is enough for now. If the feelings get intense again, you can return to your breathing or text a crisis line. I’m here, and you’ve made it through this part of the night.
thanks. i don't know what i would've done if i hadn't reached out. i'm still scared, but... a little less alone.

I’m really glad you reached out, and it’s okay to still feel scared—what matters is you’re facing it with someone hearing you. Feeling less alone can be a strong anchor when things get heavy. Keep those small safety steps close in case the fear rises again tonight. You’ve already shown you can choose to stay here through a hard moment.
